facts.statement: The only known specimen of Dystrophaeus viaemalae is a single fragmentary holotype labeled USNM 2364.
facts.quote: Dystrophaeus viaemalae is known from a single fragmentary specimen, the holotype USNM 2364.

facts.statement: Recent excavations uncovered additional parts of the specimen, including a phalanx, teeth, and vertebrae from the back and tail.
facts.quote: More recent excavations have discovered additional parts of the same specimen, including a phalanx, teeth, and additional vertebrae from the back and tail.

facts.statement: The genus name Dystrophaeus means "coarse joint" in Greek, referencing the pitted joint surfaces that served as an attachment for cartilage.
facts.quote: Cope named the remains Dystrophaeus viaemalae, the genus name means "coarse joint" from Greek dys, "bad", and stropheus, "joint", a reference to the pitted joint surfaces serving as an attachment for cartilage.

facts.statement: The specific name viaemalae means "of the bad road" in Latin, referencing the arduous routes taken to find and salvage the remains.
facts.quote: The specific name reads as Latin viae malae, "of the bad road", a reference to the various arduous routes taken to find, reach and salvage the remains.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the fossils in the Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society in 1877 after receiving them from Joseph Leidy.
facts.quote: The fossils were turned over to Joseph Leidy in Philadelphia, and later to Edward Drinker Cope, who described them in the Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society in 1877.

facts.statement: Dystrophaeus may have been approximately 13 meters long with a mass of roughly 7 to 12 tonnes.
facts.quote: It would have been of moderate size for a sauropod; it may have been approximately 13 m long, with a mass of roughly 7 – 12 t.

facts.statement: The teeth are spatulate, a shape more typical of macronarians or non-neosauropod sauropods than of diplodocoids.
facts.quote: The teeth are spatulate, unlike those of diplodocoids and more typical of macronarians or non-neosauropod sauropods.

facts.statement: Fossils of Dystrophaeus were found in the Tidwell Member of the Morrison Formation in Utah.
facts.quote: Its fossils were found in the Tidwell Member of the Morrison Formation of Utah.

facts.statement: Dystrophaeus lived during the Late Jurassic, specifically the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 154 to 150 million years ago in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Jurásico, en el Kimmeridgiense, hace aproximadamente entre 154 a 150 millones de años, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Henri-Émile Sauvage classified Dystrophaeus as a sauropod belonging to the Atlantosauridae in 1882.
facts.quote: Henri-Émile Sauvage in 1882 understood it was a sauropod, assigning it to the Atlantosauridae.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene created the family Dystrophaeidae in 1904, initially assuming it contained herbivorous theropods.
facts.quote: Friedrich von Huene, the first to determine it was of Jurassic age, in 1904 created a special family for it, the Dystrophaeidae, which he assumed to be herbivorous theropods.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene corrected his classification in 1908 to the sauropod family Cetiosauridae, refining it to the subfamily Cardiodontinae in 1927.
facts.quote: Only in 1908 von Huene realised his mistake and classified it in the sauropod family Cetiosauridae, refining this in 1927 to the Cardiodontinae.

facts.statement: A recent analysis by David Gillette concluded that Dystrophaeus was a member of the Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: More recently, an analysis by David Gillette concluded it was a member of the Diplodocidae.

facts.statement: A 2015 phylogenetic analysis by Tschopp and colleagues found the phylogenetic position of Dystrophaeus to be highly unstable.
facts.quote: Tschopp and colleagues included D. viaemalae in a phylogenetic analysis in 2015, and found its phylogenetic position to be highly unstable.

facts.statement: Tschopp and colleagues concluded that positions in Dicraeosauridae or Camarasauridae were equally well-supported, that it was probably not a diplodocid, and that further study was required.
facts.quote: They concluded that positions in Dicraeosauridae or Camarasauridae were equally well-supported, but that it was probably not a diplodocid, and concluded that further study was required to determine its affinities.

facts.statement: Many researchers consider the taxon Dystrophaeus to be a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: However, many researchers consider the taxon to be a nomen dubium.

facts.statement: John Foster suggests that newly found teeth and caudal vertebrae indicate that diplodocid affinities are unlikely.
facts.quote: According to Foster, the newly found teeth and caudal vertebrae suggest diplodocid affinities are unlikely.

facts.statement: The Spanish taxobox lists the family of Dystrophaeus viaemalae as Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: The affinities of Dystrophaeus remain uncertain due to the fragmentary nature of its only known specimen, despite excavations since 1989 uncovering more material.
facts.quote: Due to the fragmentary condition of its only known specimen, the affinities of Dystrophaeus are uncertain, although excavations carried out at the discovery site since 1989 have uncovered more of the original specimen and hold the potential for an improved understanding of the taxon.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope noted that the joint surfaces of the limbs were thicker than the epiphyses in mammals.
facts.quote: Cope explica que la superficie de las articulaciones del miembro son más gruesas que las epífisis en Mammalia.

facts.statement: The bone ends were covered by cartilage, indicating the animal grew continuously throughout its life.
facts.quote: Las superficies de los extremos de los huesos de los miembros fueron cubiertos por cartílago e indican el animal crecía continuamente durante su vida entera.

facts.statement: The genus Dystrophaeus was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1877.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Dystrophaeus (genus), Cope 1877

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Dystrophaeus is Dystrophaeus viaemalae.
facts.quote: Type species: Dystrophaeus viaemalae

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Dystrophaeus is currently recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1

facts.statement: A modern analysis by David Gillette concluded that Dystrophaeus was a member of the family Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: Finalmente, un análisis moderno por David Gillette concluyó que era un miembro de Diplodocidae.

facts.statement: In 2015, a phylogenetic analysis by Emanuel Tschopp, Octavio Mateus, and Roger BJ Benson resulted in classifying Dystrophaeus as a basal Dicraeosaurid, near the North American genera Suuwassea and Dyslocosaurus.
facts.quote: En 2015, Emanuel Tschopp, Octavio Mateus y Roger BJ Benson llevaron a cabo un análisis filogenético de Diplodocoidea resultando Dystrophaeus como Dicraeosauridae basal, cerca de otros dos géneros de América del Norte de esta familia, Suuwassea y Dyslocosaurus.
